synopsis: Dozers and graders work slowly, reverse frequently and operate close to other machines; at tip heads, dozers and loaded trucks necessarily share tight working spaces [f11432, f3355]. Heavy-machine contacts are described as the most frequently reported collision type but rank seventh by harm, whereas reversing-over incidents involving small vehicles or pedestrians rank second; the 12 August 2019 Snapper fatality involved a reversing dozer whose operator did not know a light vehicle was present [f11440, f3552, f3519, f3116]. Barrick's 2015 trial found high nuisance alarms on blades and dozers working near equipment, and operators preferred a less intrusive awareness layer, supporting the requirement not to treat every nearby truck as an emergency [f10578, f10713, f11442]. Braking validation must account for tracked-machine stopping behavior: the glossary distinguishes track grip from tire grip and identifies ISO 10265 for slow crawler machines, while manufacturer specifications put the D11 dozer at 106,614 kg, approximately 107 t [f11441, f11438, f11439, f5963, f11372]. Important evidence gaps remain: production-scale off-road vehicle-in-the-loop testing, validated automatic-braking occupant-injury curves and safe jerk limits, and exposure-adjusted collision rates by machine type were not found, so the evidence does not establish comparative machine-type risk or safe automatic-stop thresholds [f5342, f3395, f3238].
